title: Topological Sort
tagline: Ordering tasks with dependencies — the algorithm behind build systems, course prerequisites, and package managers.

sections.content:
Every time you run `npm install`, the package manager figures out which packages must be installed before which others — and does it in the right order, every time. Every time a compiler turns your source files into a binary, it decides which translation units to compile first based on which headers they import. Every university registrar system ensures you cannot enroll in Algorithms 401 before completing Data Structures 201. All of these problems share a single underlying structure: **a set of items connected by dependency relationships**, where some items cannot begin until others are finished. The algorithm that solves this class of problems elegantly and efficiently is called **topological sort**.

A **topological sort** of a directed graph produces a linear ordering of all vertices such that for every directed edge `u → v`, vertex `u` appears before vertex `v` in the ordering. Think of the edges as saying 'u must come before v.' The algorithm's job is to find an arrangement of all vertices that respects every such constraint simultaneously. This is only possible when the graph is a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** — a directed graph with no cycles. The moment you introduce a cycle (A depends on B which depends on A), no ordering can satisfy all constraints, because no matter which you place first, it violates one of its own constraints.

Two classical algorithms solve topological sorting, and both run in **O(V + E)** time — linear in the size of the graph. **Kahn's algorithm** (published 1962) works in a BFS-inspired style: it tracks how many incoming edges each vertex has (its *in-degree*), starts with vertices that have no prerequisites, and peels the graph layer by layer. The **DFS-based approach** works by running depth-first search and recording vertices in reverse finishing order — the post-order moment when all of a vertex's successors are already processed. Understanding both algorithms deeply, including *why* each one works, will give you a powerful lens for reasoning about dependency problems in system design, compilers, and distributed workflows.

This chapter covers the full story: the formal definition and prerequisites for topological sort, the complete mechanics of both algorithms with step-by-step traced examples, cycle detection as a natural byproduct, the relationship between topological order and DAG structure, common pitfalls, and real-world applications that make this algorithm genuinely important to know.

sections.title: The Construction Project Manager
sections.content:
Imagine you are managing the construction of a building. Your project has dozens of tasks: pour the foundation, frame the walls, run electrical wiring, install plumbing, hang drywall, paint, install fixtures, and do the final inspection. Many tasks have strict prerequisites: you cannot frame the walls before the foundation is set, cannot hang drywall before electrical and plumbing are roughed in, cannot paint before drywall is up.

**Kahn's algorithm is like a meticulous construction manager with a whiteboard.** At the start of the project, the manager writes down every task that has zero prerequisites — tasks that can begin immediately (pour foundation, get permits, order materials). These go on the 'ready to start' board. Each morning, the manager picks any task from the ready board, marks it as done, then goes to every task that was waiting on that completed task and crosses it off their prerequisite list. Any task whose entire prerequisite list is now crossed off moves to the ready board. This continues until all tasks are done. If tasks remain but none is ready — every remaining task is still waiting on something — there is a circular dependency, a logical impossibility in the project plan.

**The DFS-based approach is like a senior engineer who prefers to trace dependency chains end-to-end.** She picks any task, then asks: 'What does this task depend on?' She follows that chain as deep as it goes, until she reaches a task with no remaining dependencies. She schedules that foundational task first (pushes it onto the schedule), then backtracks and schedules the next deepest task, gradually working her way back up the chain. When she finally returns to the original task, all its dependencies are already scheduled, so it is safe to add it next. This depth-first, post-order scheduling naturally produces a valid topological ordering.

Both managers produce a valid construction schedule — they just reason about it differently. And both immediately notice if someone slips a circular dependency into the plan: the whiteboard manager finds tasks stuck forever on the ready board; the tracing engineer finds herself going in circles.

sections.title: What Makes a DAG — and Why Cycles Forbid Ordering
sections.content:
Before diving into the algorithms, it is worth being precise about why cycles make topological sorting impossible. Suppose you have three tasks forming a cycle: A must come before B, B must come before C, and C must come before A. Now try to produce a linear order. If you place A first, then C must come before A — contradiction. If you place B first, then A must come before B — contradiction. No matter where you start, the cycle ensures at least one edge in the cycle points 'backwards' through the ordering, violating the definition of topological sort.

This means topological sort is **defined only for DAGs**: graphs that are (1) directed — edges have a direction — and (2) acyclic — no sequence of edges leads back to its starting vertex. The acyclicity is not merely a technicality; it is the structural property that makes dependency ordering *coherent*. Real-world dependency systems are (in theory) acyclic: a package cannot depend on itself, a course cannot be its own prerequisite, a build target cannot require itself. When cycles appear in practice, they represent errors in the dependency specification, and detecting them is often just as valuable as computing the order.

**In-degree and out-degree** are key concepts. The **in-degree** of a vertex is the number of edges *coming into* it — the number of dependencies it has. A vertex with in-degree 0 has no prerequisites and can be placed at the start of any valid ordering. The **out-degree** is the number of edges leaving a vertex — how many other vertices depend on it. A vertex with out-degree 0 is a 'leaf' in the dependency sense and will always appear at the end of a valid ordering. Every DAG with at least one vertex has at least one vertex with in-degree 0 and at least one with out-degree 0 — otherwise a cycle must exist.

sections.title: Kahn's Algorithm — Step by Step
sections.content:
Arthur Kahn published his topological sorting algorithm in 1962. The algorithm is elegant because it directly operationalises the intuition: *start with things that have no prerequisites, process them, and unlock their successors*.

**Step 1: Compute in-degrees.** Build an adjacency list for the graph. Then iterate over all edges `u → v` and increment `inDegree[v]` for each. This gives you the number of unprocessed prerequisites for every vertex.

**Step 2: Seed the queue.** Add all vertices with `inDegree[v] === 0` to a queue (or any collection — order within the queue affects *which* valid topological order you get, but not *whether* you get one).

**Step 3: Process.** While the queue is non-empty: dequeue a vertex `u`, append it to the output order, then for every neighbor `v` of `u`: decrement `inDegree[v]`. If `inDegree[v]` drops to 0, enqueue `v`.

**Step 4: Check for cycles.** If the output order contains all V vertices, it is a valid topological sort. If `|output| < V`, some vertices were never enqueued — they remained trapped in a cycle where in-degrees never reached 0. In that case, the graph has a cycle and no topological sort exists.

**Why does this work?** The in-degree represents the count of *constraints not yet satisfied*. A vertex is only enqueued when all its constraints are satisfied — when every predecessor has been processed and removed from the 'pending' set. Because the graph is a DAG, processing predecessors in this order always makes progress: each processing step eliminates at least one edge, and without cycles, the in-degrees must eventually reach zero for every vertex.

**Trace on the course graph:** Start: A(0), B(0) in queue. Process A → decrement C(2→1). Process B → decrement C(1→0), D(1→0). Enqueue C, D. Process C → decrement E(1→0). Enqueue E. Process D → decrement F(2→1). Process E → decrement F(1→0). Enqueue F. Process F. Output: [A, B, C, D, E, F]. All 6 vertices included — no cycle.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Key correctness point: we check `order.length !== Object.keys(inDegree).length` rather than `nodes.length` because neighbors might not appear as keys in the original graph object. In a cycle A→B→C→A, none of A, B, C ever reaches in-degree 0, so they never enter the queue and the output is empty — length 0 versus total 3 vertices, revealing the cycle. With a queue (FIFO), you get breadth-first processing order; swapping to a stack gives depth-first processing but the result is still a valid topological sort.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    INIT["Compute in-degrees for all vertices"]
    INIT --> SEED["Enqueue vertices with in-degree = 0"]
    SEED --> DEQUEUE["Dequeue vertex u, append to order"]
    DEQUEUE --> NEIGH["For each neighbor v of u"]
    NEIGH --> DECR["Decrement in-degree of v"]
    DECR --> CHK{"in-degree of v = 0?"}
    CHK -->|"Yes"| ENQ["Enqueue v"]

    EMPTY -->|"Yes, fewer than V"| CYC["Cycle detected"]
sections.caption: Kahn's algorithm control flow. The cycle-detection step costs nothing extra — it is just a length comparison at the end. Every edge is visited exactly once (O(E)) and every vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once (O(V)).

sections.title: DFS-Based Topological Sort — The Post-Order Insight
sections.content:
The DFS-based approach emerges from a beautiful observation about depth-first search: **when DFS finishes exploring a vertex — meaning every vertex reachable from it has already been fully explored — that vertex belongs after all its successors in topological order.** Equivalently, if you push each vertex onto a stack at the moment DFS finishes with it (the *post-order* moment), then after all DFS calls are complete, popping the stack gives a valid topological order.

**Why?** Consider any edge `u → v`. When DFS processes `u`, it will recursively explore `v` (if `v` has not been visited yet). DFS will finish with `v` before it finishes with `u`, so `v` gets pushed onto the stack before `u` does. When you pop the stack (reversing push order), `u` comes out before `v`. This is exactly what topological order requires: `u` before `v` for every edge `u → v`.

**Three-color marking for cycle detection.** To detect cycles during DFS, we track three states for each vertex:
- **WHITE (unvisited):** DFS has not started here yet.
- **GREY (in-progress):** DFS has started here but not finished — this vertex is on the current recursion stack.
- **BLACK (done):** DFS has fully finished with this vertex — it and all its descendants are explored.

A **back edge** is a DFS tree edge that leads to a GREY vertex — a vertex still on the active recursion stack. A back edge means we have found a path from a vertex back to its own ancestor, which is exactly a cycle. If DFS ever encounters a GREY neighbor, the graph has a cycle and topological sort is impossible.

**Trace on the course graph:** DFS from Calculus → Linear Algebra → Algorithms (no more neighbors, BLACK, push Algorithms) → LINEAR ALGEBRA done (BLACK, push Linear Algebra) → CALCULUS done (BLACK, push Calculus). DFS from Intro CS → Data Structures → Algorithms already BLACK, skip → Data Structures done (push Data Structures) → Intro CS done (push Intro CS). Stack bottom-to-top: [Algorithms, Linear Algebra, Calculus, Data Structures, Intro CS]. Reversed: [Intro CS, Data Structures, Calculus, Linear Algebra, Algorithms] — a valid topological order.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The three-color scheme is the key to cycle detection. WHITE → GREY when DFS enters a node; GREY → BLACK when DFS exits it. A GREY node encountered as a neighbor means we have found a path from an ancestor to itself — a cycle. Iterating over all nodes in the outer loop ensures correctness even on disconnected graphs (multiple separate components). The `verifyTopologicalOrder` helper is excellent for testing your implementation: it checks every edge to confirm the source appears before the destination.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> WHITE
    WHITE --> GREY : DFS enters node
    GREY --> BLACK : DFS exits node (push to stack)
    BLACK --> BLACK : already done, skip
    GREY --> CYCLE : neighbor is GREY (back edge found)
sections.caption: The three-state DFS color scheme. A vertex transitions WHITE → GREY when DFS first visits it, and GREY → BLACK when DFS fully finishes with it. Finding a GREY neighbor is the cycle-detection signal — it means that neighbor is an ancestor of the current node.

sections.title: Comparing the Two Algorithms — When to Use Which
sections.content:
Both Kahn's algorithm and DFS-based topological sort run in O(V + E) time and O(V + E) space (for storing the graph, in-degrees, and visited state). For most practical purposes, they are interchangeable. But there are real differences worth knowing.

**Kahn's algorithm advantages:**
- **Iterative, not recursive.** This is significant for very large graphs: deep DFS can cause stack overflow if recursion depth exceeds the call stack limit. Kahn's uses a queue and a simple while-loop — no recursion, no stack overflow risk.
- **Naturally detects cycles via count.** The cycle check is a single integer comparison at the end. No need for the three-color tracking scheme.
- **Easy to understand and verify.** The in-degree invariant is straightforward: a vertex enters the queue *if and only if* all its predecessors have been processed.
- **Can emit vertices in a controlled order.** If you use a priority queue (min-heap) instead of a plain queue, Kahn's will produce the *lexicographically smallest* (or any other sorted) topological order. This matters for problems that ask for the unique lexicographically minimum schedule.

**DFS-based algorithm advantages:**
- **More compact to implement.** The recursive DFS with a stack is concise and elegant — easy to write from memory during an interview.
- **Integrates naturally with other DFS-based computations.** If you are already running DFS for some other purpose (strongly connected components via Tarjan's, finding bridges, etc.), you can compute topological order as a side effect with no extra passes.
- **Intuitive correctness argument.** The post-order intuition — 'push after exploring all successors' — directly maps to the definition of topological sort.

**The key interview insight:** In a whiteboard setting, if the question asks for topological sort, reach for Kahn's algorithm first — the BFS approach is slightly easier to trace through step-by-step and the cycle detection is trivially explained. If the question is already in a DFS context (e.g., 'find cycles and ordering'), use the three-color DFS approach.

sections.title: Multiple Valid Orderings and Unique Orderings
sections.content:
An important subtlety: **topological sort does not produce a unique answer in general.** Whenever two vertices have no dependency relationship between them (neither can reach the other), either can appear first in a valid topological ordering. The number of valid orderings can be exponential in the number of independent vertices.

For example, in a graph where A → C and B → C but there is no edge between A and B: both [A, B, C] and [B, A, C] are valid topological orders. When Kahn's algorithm processes this graph, both A and B start with in-degree 0, so both enter the queue. The order in which they are dequeued determines which valid ordering you get.

**When is the topological order unique?** If and only if the DAG has a **Hamiltonian path** — a path that visits every vertex exactly once. In that case, at every step of Kahn's algorithm, exactly one vertex has in-degree 0, leaving no choice. This is equivalent to the graph having a unique topological sort, which can be verified by checking that the queue contains at most one element at every step during Kahn's algorithm.

**Uniqueness has algorithmic applications.** Some problems (like checking if a sequence is the *only* valid build order) rely on detecting when the topological order is forced. If you run Kahn's and find the queue always has exactly one element, the ordering is uniquely determined.

**Practical consequence for reproducibility:** If your build system or test runner uses topological sort and the result depends on which of multiple valid orderings is chosen, you might get different behavior across runs if the graph structure changes even slightly. This is a real source of non-determinism bugs in large systems. Using a priority queue (to always pick the lexicographically smallest ready vertex) makes the ordering deterministic and reproducible.

sections.title: Real-World Applications in Depth
sections.content:
Topological sort is one of those algorithms that appears in a surprisingly wide range of real systems, often hiding under different names.

**Build systems (Make, Bazel, CMake, Gradle).** Every build system represents source files and generated artifacts as a DAG. File A depends on header B means the edge B → A in the DAG. The build system runs topological sort to determine compilation order. Critically, **parallel builds** are a direct application: instead of processing one vertex at a time, a parallel build system processes all 'currently ready' vertices (those with in-degree 0) simultaneously across multiple CPU cores. The in-degree queue in Kahn's algorithm naturally represents this ready set.

**Package managers (npm, pip, cargo, apt).** When you install a package, the package manager must install its transitive dependencies first. The dependency graph is a DAG (package managers reject circular dependencies). Topological sort determines the installation order. The algorithm must also handle version constraints, but the ordering problem is pure topological sort.

**Task scheduling and workflow engines.** Apache Airflow, Luigi, and Prefect — all popular workflow orchestration systems — represent data pipelines as DAGs. Each step is a vertex; an edge from step A to step B means 'run A before B.' Topological sort finds the execution order. Parallel execution of independent steps is a direct application.

**Compiler optimizations.** In a compiler's intermediate representation, **data-flow analysis** and **instruction scheduling** use topological sort on basic block dependency graphs. Instructions that do not depend on each other can be reordered (or executed in parallel on a CPU with out-of-order execution) — a form of parallelism derived from topological analysis.

**Spreadsheet evaluation order.** A spreadsheet with formulas in cells forms a DAG (cell A1 references B1 means edge B1 → A1). When you change a value, the spreadsheet engine uses topological sort to determine which cells need recalculation and in what order — only cells 'downstream' of the changed cell, in dependency order.

**Course scheduling and academic prerequisite validation.** University systems represent courses and prerequisites as a DAG and use topological sort to verify that curriculum plans are consistent (no circular prerequisites) and to suggest valid enrollment sequences.

**Deadlock detection in operating systems.** Resource allocation graphs, where processes and resources are vertices and 'waiting for' / 'held by' edges connect them, can be analyzed using DFS cycle detection — the same algorithm underlying DFS topological sort. A cycle in the resource allocation graph means a deadlock.

**Historical context:** Kahn's algorithm was published by Arthur B. Kahn in 1962 in the *Communications of the ACM*, in a paper titled 'Topological Sorting of Large Networks.' The DFS-based approach was implicit in Tarjan's 1972 algorithm for strongly connected components and was later formalized as a standalone technique. The problem of ordering tasks with dependencies was studied even earlier — PERT charts (Program Evaluation and Review Technique), developed by the U.S. Navy in 1958 for managing the Polaris missile program, rely on the same DAG-ordering concepts. The critical path in a project plan — the longest dependency chain that determines minimum project duration — is computed on the topologically sorted DAG.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Mistake 1: Forgetting that topological sort requires a DAG.** If you run topological sort on an undirected graph (or treat a directed graph as undirected), the results are meaningless. Topological sort is specifically for *directed* graphs where edge direction encodes the 'must come before' relationship. On an undirected graph, the concept of 'topological order' does not exist.

**Mistake 2: Confusing which direction the edge should point.** There are two common conventions: (a) edge `u → v` means 'u must come before v' (u is a prerequisite of v), and (b) edge `u → v` means 'u depends on v' (v must come before u). Convention (a) is more natural for topological sort because vertices with in-degree 0 are processed first. Convention (b) requires reversing the final order. Pick a convention and be consistent — bugs from edge-direction confusion are subtle and common.

**Mistake 3: Not handling disconnected graphs.** A graph can have multiple connected components. In Kahn's algorithm, all zero-in-degree vertices from all components enter the initial queue, so disconnected graphs are handled automatically. In DFS-based sort, the outer loop must iterate over *all* vertices (not just start DFS from one), so that all components are explored. Forgetting this causes some components to be silently omitted from the output.

**Mistake 4: Off-by-one in cycle detection.** In Kahn's algorithm, the cycle check `order.length !== V` must compare against the *total* number of vertices, including any that may be neighbors not listed as keys in the adjacency list. Carefully handle the case where a vertex appears as a neighbor but has no outgoing edges (and thus no key in the adjacency list).

**Mistake 5: Pre-order vs. post-order in DFS.** Pushing a vertex to the stack when DFS *enters* it (pre-order) does NOT produce a topological sort. You must push when DFS *exits* it (post-order, after all successors are fully explored). This is the single most common mistake in implementing DFS-based topological sort from scratch.

**Edge case: Empty graph.** An empty graph (no vertices) trivially has an empty topological order. A graph with vertices but no edges has a valid topological order (any permutation of vertices), since all vertices have in-degree 0.

**Edge case: Self-loops.** A self-loop (edge from u to u) is a cycle of length 1. It makes topological sort impossible for that vertex. In Kahn's algorithm, a self-loop means u's in-degree is at least 1 even at initialization, so it is never enqueued — correctly detected as a cycle participant.

**Interview tips and common question patterns:**
- 'Course Schedule' (LeetCode 207, 210) is the canonical topological sort interview problem. Problem 207 asks if a valid order exists (cycle detection); Problem 210 asks for the actual order. Both are solved directly by Kahn's algorithm.
- When asked 'is this possible?' (can we complete all courses?), the answer is 'yes iff the graph is a DAG' — use Kahn's cycle detection.
- When asked 'in what order?', output the topological sort result from Kahn's or DFS.
- If the question asks for the *lexicographically smallest* topological order, use Kahn's with a min-heap (priority queue) instead of a regular queue.
- If in-degree or out-degree is mentioned in the problem, that is a strong hint toward Kahn's algorithm.
- If the problem mentions 'finish time' or 'discovery time' in a DFS context, the DFS approach is more natural.
- Always check: does the graph need to be built from an edge list first? Parse edges, build adjacency list, then run topological sort — the full pipeline is what you will implement in almost every real interview.

items: **Topological sort** produces a linear ordering of a DAG's vertices where every edge `u → v` has u before v. It is only possible on Directed Acyclic Graphs — any cycle makes consistent ordering logically impossible.

**Kahn's algorithm** (BFS-style): compute in-degrees, seed a queue with in-degree-0 vertices, process vertices by decrementing neighbor in-degrees and enqueuing those that reach 0. Cycle detected when `|output| < V`. Time: O(V + E).

**DFS-based sort**: run DFS with three-color marking (WHITE/GREY/BLACK), push each vertex to a stack at post-order (DFS exit), reverse the stack. Cycle detected when a GREY neighbor is found (back edge). Time: O(V + E).

**Multiple valid orderings** exist whenever independent vertices have no constraint between them. Use a min-heap in Kahn's for the lexicographically smallest ordering. The order is unique iff the DAG has a Hamiltonian path (queue always has exactly one ready vertex).

**Real-world applications** include npm/pip package installation, Make/Bazel build systems, Apache Airflow workflow DAGs, spreadsheet formula evaluation, compiler instruction scheduling, and university course prerequisite validation.

**Kahn's is preferred in practice** for large graphs (no recursion stack overflow risk) and when a specific ordering (e.g., lexicographic minimum) is needed. DFS-based is more compact and integrates naturally with other DFS algorithms.

**Common mistakes to avoid**: using pre-order instead of post-order in DFS sort, confusing edge direction conventions, forgetting to iterate all vertices for disconnected graph components, and not accounting for self-loops as trivial cycles.

quiz.question: On what type of graph is topological sort defined, and why?
options: Any connected graph, because connectivity guarantees an ordering exists
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) only, because a cycle creates contradictory ordering constraints that cannot be satisfied
Weighted directed graphs, because weights determine the ordering priority
Undirected graphs with at least one spanning tree
quiz.explanation: Topological sort requires a DAG. In a cycle A→B→C→A, the constraints say A before B, B before C, and C before A — which is impossible to satisfy simultaneously in any linear ordering. Every DAG with at least one vertex has at least one vertex with in-degree 0, which provides a valid starting point for the ordering.

quiz.question: In Kahn's algorithm, which vertices are placed in the initial queue?
options: Vertices with the highest out-degree (most dependents)
Vertices with in-degree equal to zero (no prerequisites)
The single source vertex if the graph is connected
Vertices in alphabetical order regardless of their in-degree
quiz.explanation: Vertices with in-degree 0 have no incoming edges — no prerequisites. They can be legally placed first in any topological ordering. These are the only valid 'start' vertices. In a course scheduling example, these are courses with no prerequisites, and they seed the queue. Processing them first then exposes their successors.

quiz.question: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle in the graph?
options: It runs a second DFS pass after completing the BFS to look for back edges
If the output order contains fewer vertices than the total vertex count V, a cycle exists
It checks whether any vertex has in-degree greater than its out-degree
It verifies that the last vertex in the output has out-degree 0
quiz.explanation: Vertices involved in a cycle never reach in-degree 0, because they always have at least one incoming edge from another vertex in the cycle. They are never enqueued and never appear in the output. After the algorithm finishes, if the output has fewer than V vertices, those missing vertices are trapped in cycles. This makes cycle detection a free byproduct of running Kahn's algorithm.

quiz.question: In DFS-based topological sort, when exactly is a vertex pushed onto the result stack?
options: When DFS first visits the vertex (pre-order, before exploring any neighbors)
When DFS finishes exploring all of the vertex's successors (post-order, on exit)
When the vertex's in-degree first reaches zero during the traversal
When DFS backtracks from the vertex to its parent in the DFS tree
quiz.explanation: A vertex is pushed in post-order — after all vertices reachable from it are fully explored and already on the stack. This guarantees that when the stack is reversed, every vertex appears before all vertices it has edges to. Pre-order pushing (on entry) would place a vertex before its predecessors are processed, which is incorrect.

quiz.question: What is a 'back edge' in DFS, and what does finding one indicate for topological sort?
options: An edge connecting two vertices in different DFS trees — indicates the graph is disconnected
An edge from a vertex to an ancestor currently on the active recursion stack (a GREY vertex) — indicates a cycle
An edge from a vertex with high out-degree to a leaf vertex — safe to ignore
An edge that goes in the reverse direction of the topological order — can be removed to fix the sort
quiz.explanation: A back edge in DFS connects a vertex to an ancestor that is still being explored (marked GREY — currently on the active recursion stack). This means there is a path from the ancestor down to the current vertex (through the DFS tree) AND now an edge back from the current vertex to that ancestor — forming a cycle. The presence of any back edge means topological sort is impossible for this graph.

quiz.question: Graph edges: A→C, B→C, B→D, C→E, D→F, E→F. How many valid topological orderings exist that place both A and B before C?
options: Exactly one: A, B, C, D, E, F
Exactly two: [A,B,C,D,E,F] and [B,A,C,D,E,F]
Three or more, because D and E are also independent of each other
None — a valid ordering where both A and B precede C is impossible
quiz.explanation: A and B are independent (neither has an edge to the other), so either can come first: [A,B,...] or [B,A,...]. After processing C, we have D and E both ready (C→E is satisfied and B→D was already satisfied when B was processed). D and E are independent of each other, so we also get [A,B,C,D,E,F] or [A,B,C,E,D,F] or [B,A,C,D,E,F] or [B,A,C,E,D,F] — at least four valid orderings.

quiz.question: Under what condition does a DAG have exactly one valid topological ordering?
options: When every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge
When the DAG has a Hamiltonian path — a path visiting every vertex exactly once
When all edge weights are distinct
When the graph has no vertices with in-degree greater than 1
quiz.explanation: The topological ordering is unique if and only if the DAG has a Hamiltonian path — a path that visits every vertex exactly once. In this case, at every step of Kahn's algorithm, exactly one vertex has in-degree 0, leaving no choice. Equivalently: in the sorted sequence, every consecutive pair of vertices has a direct edge between them. If at any point two or more vertices simultaneously have in-degree 0, multiple valid orderings exist.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of both Kahn's and DFS-based topological sort?
options: O(V log V) due to the queue operations
O(V + E) — linear in vertices and edges
O(V · E) because each vertex inspects all edges
O(E log E) when using a priority queue for ordering
quiz.explanation: Both algorithms are O(V + E). In Kahn's: every vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once (O(V)), and every edge is examined exactly once when processing its source vertex (O(E)). In DFS: each vertex is visited once (O(V)) and each edge is traversed once (O(E)). Note: using a priority queue instead of a regular queue in Kahn's makes it O((V + E) log V) for the lexicographically-ordered variant.

quiz.question: A parallel build system wants to compile as many files as possible simultaneously. Which data structure in Kahn's algorithm directly represents the set of files ready to compile at any moment?
options: The in-degree array, which shows which files have the fewest dependencies
The queue (or set) of vertices with current in-degree 0
The output order list, which grows as files are compiled
The adjacency list, which lists all compilation dependencies
quiz.explanation: In Kahn's algorithm, the queue contains exactly the vertices whose in-degree has reached 0 — all prerequisites have been satisfied. For a parallel build system, these are exactly the files that can be compiled right now. Instead of dequeuing one at a time, a parallel build system dequeues all of them and compiles in parallel. Each time a compilation finishes, its successors' in-degrees are decremented, potentially adding more files to the ready set.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes a key practical difference between Kahn's and DFS-based topological sort?
options: Kahn's can handle cyclic graphs and produce a partial order; DFS requires a DAG
Kahn's is iterative with no recursion risk; DFS is recursive and can overflow the call stack on very deep graphs
DFS-based sort runs in O(V + E) but Kahn's requires O(E log E) due to in-degree sorting
Kahn's always produces the unique lexicographic minimum ordering; DFS produces all possible orderings
quiz.explanation: Kahn's algorithm uses a queue and a while-loop — no recursion at all. For very deep or large graphs (V in the millions), DFS recursion can exhaust the call stack (typically limited to tens of thousands of frames). Kahn's avoids this entirely and is therefore preferred in production systems handling large dependency graphs. Both detect cycles, both run in O(V + E), and neither always produces a unique or all orderings without additional constraints.
